topics.title: Rendering and re-renders
topics.notes: Crazy how 'prop chnages' are not why React components re-render and it's actually due to state changes. Apparently prop chnages is a common misconception. Most times when a component's prop changes, it's because the parent's state changed and that's what's actually causing the re-render

topics.title: Effects, and when not to use them
topics.notes: Only watched the video and not the reading. Still learned that useEffects should not be a go to for everything. They should be used when you need to do something after a render, like fetching data or updating the DOM. If you can do it during render, then do it during render like event-specific logic.

topics.title: Refs, reducers, and custom hooks
topics.notes: useReducer can be used to manage state and state actions in a modular way. (Refer to screenshot "useReducerExample.png") useRef can be used to store mutable values that do not cause re-renders when updated. Custom hooks can be used to extract and reuse logic across components.

topics.title: Context
topics.notes: Can be used to pass data down the component tree without having to pass props down manually at every level. It can be used for global state management, theming, and more. You can use useReducer with useContext (create a context that holds state and one that holds dispatch).

topics.title: Memoization and the React Compiler
topics.notes: There was an update in Dec 2024 to the React compiler so that your code iss automatically memoized upon build. This means that you no longer have to use React.memo or useMemo in most cases. The compiler will automatically memoize your components and hooks for you. This is a huge performance improvement and will make your code faster and more efficient.

topics.title: What's new in React 19
topics.notes: React 19 includes a lot of support for async rendering, including Suspense and use() for data fetching, useAction() for handling data fetching actions, and a new concurrent mode that allows React to interrupt rendering to work on other tasks. This will make your app more responsive and improve the user experience. Could go back and look into this more.

topics.title: Mocking the network, and testing hooks
Week 1 - Demo project
topics.notes: Broke it a lot along the way. Mapping out your variables really is a lot to consider. Removed the key from a React list and saw that it still rendered just with some errors.

questions.question: What's the difference between data from a server and state that only lives in the app?
questions.answer: Server data lives in the database, and the app only holds a cached copy that can go stale, so it has to be fetched, cached, refetched and kept in sync. In this app that's the topics and the current week, handled by TanStack Query. App-only state, like the search text, the active tab or which page is open, exists only in the browser and is owned by React (useState or context). Nothing outside the app can change it.

questions.question: What's an optimistic update, and what happens when it fails?
questions.answer: You update the screen right away as if the save already worked, instead of waiting for the server. Here, clicking a status icon saves a snapshot of the topics, then writes the new status into the cache in onMutate. If the PUT fails, onError puts the snapshot back, so the task jumps back to its old tab. Either way, onSettled refetches to match the server.

questions.question: What does an error boundary catch, and what doesn't it catch?
questions.answer: It catches errors thrown while rendering the components below it, including in lifecycle methods and constructors, and a useSuspenseQuery whose fetch fails. It doesn't catch errors in event handlers, in async code like setTimeout or a fetch in useEffect, in server-side rendering, or in the boundary itself. Mutation errors don't reach it unless you rethrow them during render.

questions.question: Why would you load part of an app only when it's needed?
questions.answer: So the first load is smaller and faster. Code for a page the user might never open, like Stats or this Flashcards page, goes into its own chunk with lazy() and is only downloaded when it first renders. Suspense shows a fallback while that chunk loads.

questions.question: What's a compound component? Show me yours.
questions.answer: A parent component plus child parts that share state through context, so you arrange the pieces however you like instead of passing lots of props. Mine is TopicCard: <TopicCard topic={task}> puts the topic and setStatus into context, and TopicCard.Header, TopicCard.Status and TopicCard.Notes read from it. TaskList puts Header and Status in one row and Notes underneath.

questions.question: What's a monorepo, and why would a company use one?
questions.answer: One git repository holding many projects, like several apps and the libraries they share. Companies use one so shared code changes in a single commit instead of being published and bumped across repos, everyone uses the same tooling and dependency versions, and a change that breaks another team's app shows up before it's merged. The cost is that builds and tests get slow without a tool like Nx to only run what's needed.

questions.question: What's the difference between an app and a library in Nx?
questions.answer: An app is something you build and deploy on its own, like this learning-tracker React app, and it's where code gets put together. A library is a reusable piece of code that apps (or other libraries) import, like UI components, data hooks or utilities. Nx encourages thin apps and most code in libraries, so it can be shared, tested on its own and cached separately.

questions.question: How does Nx know what's "affected" by a change?
questions.answer: It compares your files against a base commit (usually main) to see what changed, then works out which projects own those files. It uses the project graph, built by reading imports and package.json dependencies, to find every project that depends on those projects, directly or indirectly. Those are the affected ones, so nx affected -t test only tests them.

questions.question: Why would you forbid some parts of the code from importing others?
questions.answer: To keep the architecture from tangling as the repo grows. For example, a shared UI library shouldn't import from one specific app, and one team's feature shouldn't reach into another team's internals. Nx does this with tags on projects and the @nx/enforce-module-boundaries lint rule, so a bad import fails lint instead of quietly creating a dependency that's hard to undo.

questions.question: What is caching saving you, in plain terms?
questions.answer: Time spent redoing work you've already done. Before running a task like build or test, Nx hashes its inputs (the source files, config and dependencies). If it has run with exactly those inputs before, it replays the saved output and logs instead of running it again. With remote caching, a teammate or CI that already ran it can save you the run too.

questions.question: Why test what the user sees instead of how the code works inside?
questions.answer: Because that's what actually has to keep working. A test that finds a button by its role and text and clicks it keeps passing when you refactor the inside, like swapping useState for useReducer, and fails only when the user would notice something broken. Tests that check internal state or which function was called break on every refactor, even when nothing is wrong for the user.

questions.question: What's jsdom, and why do your tests need it? Name something it can't do.
questions.answer: jsdom is a JavaScript version of the browser's DOM that runs in Node. Tests run in Node, which has no document or window, so React Testing Library needs jsdom to render components and fire clicks. It doesn't do layout or painting: getBoundingClientRect returns zeros and CSS isn't applied, so it can't tell you whether the flip cards actually flip or whether the toggle is centered.

questions.question: What's the difference between jest.fn, jest.spyOn, and jest.mock?
questions.answer: jest.fn() makes a new fake function you pass in yourself, like an onClick prop, and records how it was called. jest.spyOn(object, 'method') wraps a method that already exists, like fetch or console.error, so you can watch it or replace what it returns, and restore it afterwards. jest.mock('module') replaces a whole imported module for the test file. This project uses Vitest, where they're vi.fn, vi.spyOn and vi.mock.

questions.question: When would you mock a whole module, and when would you fake the network with MSW instead?
questions.answer: Mock a module when it's something you don't want running in the test at all and the network isn't the point, like an analytics SDK, a date library or a heavy chart component. Use MSW when the code talks to an API: it intercepts the real requests, so your fetch code, error handling and TanStack Query hooks all run for real against fake responses. That catches bugs a mocked hook would hide, like forgetting to check res.ok.

questions.question: Show me a bug one of your tests would catch.
questions.answer: TopicsErrorBoundary.spec.tsx makes the topics fetch return a 500, checks the "Couldn't load topics" card appears, clicks "Try again" and checks the topics load. If the boundary stopped calling TanStack's reset() before re-rendering, the query would stay in its error state, the card would never go away and the test would fail. It would also fail if useTopics stopped checking res.ok: the empty 500 response would blow up later in res.json() with a vague parse error instead of "GET /topics failed: 500", and the test checks for that message.
